title: Miriam daughter of Bilgah
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: The end of Tosefta Sukkah and the Gemara there relate that during Greek rule, before the Hasmoneans arose, she abandoned her religion and married a soldier of the Greek monarchy. When the Greeks entered the Sanctuary, Miriam struck the top of the altar, saying: “Lokos, Lokos! You have consumed Israel’s property and did not stand by them in their distress.” Therefore Bilgah’s priestly watch always had its ring fixed and its window sealed.
Hyman explains that Bilgah was not her father’s name: it was one of the Temple’s twenty-four priestly watches, the fifteenth, as stated in I Chronicles, chapter 24.
And she was of their family.

notes.text: The supplied notice says she struck the altar; the sandal detail in the primary account is not inserted into this translation. Bilgah is explained by Hyman as the priestly watch, not her father’s name. The address Lokos remains in transliteration.

The consulted Sukkah 56b has Miriam daughter of Bilgah kicking the altar with her sandal, and then distinguishes her father and mother from the whole priestly watch when explaining collective punishment. Hyman’s statement that Bilgah is the watch rather than her father’s name is retained as his explanation. The omitted sandal detail is not inserted into his supplied text, and no new genealogy is admitted.
